render.title: Cristae remodelling during apoptosis
render.body:
Yes, the cristae folds do change shape during cell death (apoptosis), and this remodelling is controlled by specific proteins.

Under normal conditions, the inner mitochondrial membrane is folded into cristae, which are sealed at their openings (crista junctions) by ring-shaped oligomers of a protein called OPA1. This sealing keeps cytochrome c — a small electron carrier — trapped inside the cristae, where it normally shuttles electrons between Complex III and Complex IV.

When a cell receives signals to undergo apoptosis, two proteins called BAX and BAK become activated. BAX and BAK are members of the BCL-2 family and are inserted into the outer mitochondrial membrane. Their activation triggers the opening of the crista junctions by disrupting the OPA1 oligomers. The cristae unfold and widen, releasing the stored cytochrome c into the intermembrane space.

Cytochrome c can then pass through pores formed by BAX/BAK in the outer membrane and enter the cytoplasm. Once in the cytoplasm, cytochrome c joins with other proteins to form the apoptosome, which activates enzymes called caspases that carry out the destruction of the cell.

In summary:
- OPA1 normally keeps crista junctions sealed and cytochrome c confined.
- BAX and BAK activation opens the junctions and remodels the cristae.
- This releases cytochrome c, triggering the cell death cascade.

This connection between cristae structure and apoptosis shows that the physical shape of the inner membrane is not just about maximising ATP output — it also serves as a regulated checkpoint in cell survival decisions.
render.summary: During apoptosis, BAX and BAK proteins disrupt OPA1 oligomers that normally seal crista junctions, causing the cristae to open and release cytochrome c into the cytoplasm, where it triggers the caspase cascade that executes cell death.
